senses: Written in an artistic style or manner, as calligraphy.
Ski mountaineering, especially competitive ski mountaineering.
Having bristles
ety: From Middle English bristled, ibrustled, iburstled, equivalent to bristle + -ed.

senses: A parasitic fungus of trees, usually birch, found on the circumboreal region of the Northern hemisphere, Inonotus obliquus.
The irregular conk of this fungus, used in East European folk medicine to treat a number of conditions.
ety: Borrowed from Russian ча́га (čága), Komi-Zyrian тшак (čak, “mushroom, growth”).

senses: In early Vedas, a cosmic man whose sacrifice by the gods created all life.
In the Upanishad, an abstract essence of self, spirit, and the Universal Principle that is eternal, without form and all-pervasive, distinguished from the mutable material world.
The process by which an organism produces others of its biological kind
The sexual activity of conceiving and bearing biological offspring
ety: From Old French procreacion, from Latin prōcreātiō (“generation”), the noun of action from prōcreāre (“to bring forth”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + creāre (“to create”). First attested in c. 1386.

senses: Something that is characteristic of the western part of a region.
A person who lives in, or comes from, a village.
A worker unit.
A deficiency in understanding, processing, or describing emotions.
ety: From a- + lexi + -thymia. Created by psychiatrists John Case Nemiah and Peter Sifneos from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + λέξις (léxis, “speaking”) + θυμός (thumós, “heart”), meaning “without words for emotions”.

senses: Having the ability to absorb a great amount of fluid relative to its own mass.
A gathering of like-minded people protesting for a cause.
A person who jousts.
A horse used as a mount when jousting.
Created unofficially by enthusiasts.
A scientist whose speciality is neuroscience.
A pedophile.
ety: From pedo + bear. First widespread use dates to 2009.

senses: The fruit of the wax myrtle shrub; or the plant itself (Morella cerifera), with aromatic, leathery leaves and waxy berries.
The fruit of the bay laurel (Laurus nobilis).
West Indian bay tree (Pimenta racemosa), a tropical American shrub with aromatic leaves that are used in the preparation of bay rum.
examples: It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

senses: A person or device that toots; a pipe or horn, or the person who plays it.
Of a stringed instrument, not having frets on the fingerboard.
Without worries.
examples: You would live longer and happier if you would only be quiet and fretless.
Will the fretless world be happy or will restless nature shout / For some old-time fret or worry just to rave and kick about?
Is it not worth while to try and approximate, if we cannot hope to attain, the ideal of fretless, fussless, and unworrying poise?

senses: A nobody; a person of no importance.
examples: A quidam gallant determined upon a time to surprise both my house and my selfe.
She singing a miserable ditty, a bead-roll of lamentable rhymes, strung together by this Quidam!—This Henley!

senses: homebrew alcohol; moonshine
That lives within a body or cells of another organism. Forming an endosymbiosis.
To twinkle; to sparkle.
ety: From Middle English twinken, twynken, from Old English *twincian (“to wink; twinkle”), from Proto-West Germanic *twinkōn, from Proto-Germanic *twinkōną, an augmented form (with formative *-kōną; see English -k) of Proto-Germanic *twint- (“to twinkle”). Cognate with Middle High German zwinken, zwingen, modern German zwinkern (“to wink; twinkle”), Middle Dutch twinc (“a blink”), Middle High German zwinzen, zwinzern (“to blink, blink hard”).

senses: Of or containing pebbles.
With a surface like that of pebbles.
examples: The balance of that day we spent in continuing a minute and fruitless exploration of the monotonous coast. There was not another break in the frowning cliffs--not even another minute patch of pebbly beach.
Mr Rottcodd turned his pebbly eyes away.

senses: The scholarly or scientific study of music, as in historical research, music theory, or the physical nature of sound.
To make or become mild or milder.
One who assists; an assistant or helper.
Able to accommodate multiple uses.
examples: The new stadium and park would be lined on three sides with multiuse row house buildings containing commercial, office, and loft residential space.

senses: The quality of being unhealthful or diseased, sometimes including the cause.
The quality of being morbid; an attitude or state of mind marked by gloom.
The sickness rate of a population.
ety: Recorded since 1721; from morbid + -ity, from Latin morbidus (“diseased”), from morbus (“disease”), from the root of morī (“to die”) or from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to rub, pound, wear away”).
examples: He taught him how to be superior to human foibles and how to give a godlike laugh at himself as a way of fending off morbidity. He did all the things for him that a woman is grateful for, except that Magnus is a man.

senses: A publication in which a work is serialized.
An electronic device that converts a parallel stream of data into serial format.
examples: The Saturday Evening Post, serializer of six novels by David Graham Phillips, climbed to one million circulation by 1910.

senses: A greasy yellow substance chemically akin to wax that is secreted from wooly animals, with a variety of uses from rust prevention, lubrication and waterproofing to cosmetics and skin ointments.
Full of nuggets.
Having the characteristics of a nugget.
Short, stocky, and powerful.
examples: Nuggety veins are characterized by localized, erratic, high-grades and coarse-free gold.
Mikli (1986) does not recommend plate pulverizers for the final pulverizing of nuggety gold ores, as the plate pulverizer does not significantly reduce the particle size of gold nuggets.
Like the old miners, I camped in the nuggety gully.

senses: To collect mussels, clams, etc. in shallow water using one's hands.
ety: From earlier polwigge, from Middle English polwygle, equal to poll (“head”) + wiggle.
examples: I grew up on the Mississippi River and as a youth I fished, camped, and pollywogged for clams on the river, but I never found a pearl.

senses: Able to be customized.
A community of runaway slaves.
ety: From Spanish Palenque, the name of a maroon settlement in Colombia, from palenque (“palisade”).
examples: Different from dozens of other palenques that were vanquished, this community has successfully fended off threats to its existence to this day.

senses: An engineered path to channel floodwaters away from areas to be protected.
examples: Since 2005 the governments of Manitoba and Canada have spent $665 million to double the capacity of the floodway and to reinforce bridges, control gates and dikes.

senses: An old Saxon and Welsh form of tenure by which an estate passed, on the holder's death, to all the sons equally; also called gavelkind.
ety: From Middle English gavel, from Old English gafol, from Proto-West Germanic *gabul, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną (“to give”), equivalent to give + -el.

senses: The act, or an instance, of depressurizing; a reduction of atmospheric pressure within a chamber or space vehicle etc.
The acorn or mast of the oak and similar fruits.
Having the character of a caricature.
In Ancient Rome, a small box for holding incense.
In Ancient Rome, a small sacrificial altar.
